utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think that the Defence wished to make submissions as a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We were required to state our position on a document within 48 hours. This is document that was used in the testimony of Witness Grujo Boric, 65 ter 32447. I would just like to use the opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence has no objection to this document being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then decide in due course on the admission. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which would be, if I understand well, Mr. Ratko Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Melikian, you'll cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic standing to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, for the purposes of the transcript, to slowly state your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ratko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Trial Chamber where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Opravdici on the 12th of July, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which schools you completed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school. That's eight years of school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you serve your military term of duty? And if you did, when and where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I served my military term of duty from 1964 to 1967, 11 months in Gnjilane and 10 months in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you employed just before the war broke out in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was working in the 21st of May in Rakovica, Belgrade. And it was the basic unit in Zvornik of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Trial Chamber in which republic Mali Zvornik is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mali Zvornik is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I worked as a security personnel. I was working at the reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have any weapons as part of your duties as a reception guard?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We did have weapons which -- a weapon which we handed over at the end and beginning of each shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the village where you lived, were you personally drafted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber why you were not mobilised by the army in that period, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was not mobilised because each worker had to be registered at the work organisation and in the municipality where he worked. That's where he was registered as a permanent resident. So you had to be registered with the SUP and with your company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And will you tell the Trial Chamber where you were at the time -- where you were registered at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was registered in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And at that initial period of the war, were you living in your village or did you live in Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Until 1992, I commuted to work. I think that was until August when the barricades started to be set up on the road to Zvornik. After that, I couldn't commute anymore. I had a brother, so for another month or so I worked. After that the company, the director dismissed us to go home, and we received a minimal salary from the company because war was already underway and a lot of workers were dismissed and they were staying at home. I couldn't come to work because of the problems in commuting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you start to permanently live in your village of Opravdici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think I went back to my village for good in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, could you please tell us August of which year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: August 1993. That was the year when they burned us. Actually, it was August 1992. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, could you please tell us again: August of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the ethnic composition of your village, Opravdici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Our village of Opravdici was a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And was Opravdici a part of a larger Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a part of a larger Serbian village. That was the population. It had perhaps a hundred or 150 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the neighbouring village where the centre of that area is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of the village of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you observe or did you at any time become active in the protection and the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were on guard duty for a little bit because my village is close to the centre. It's about a kilometre away from Kravica. There were people that we didn't know who were coming in, walking around there, so anything could have happened because just the women were there and elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you have any weapons which you used for these duties?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, there was an elderly man who had a hunting rifle, so he carried that around for a little bit, but I didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time, from August 1992 until January 1993, did any fighting go on near your village and near Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, because Muslim forces were attacking the area around Srebrenica, so all the neighbouring villages were burned and anybody that they encountered, they killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the able-bodied men from your village at that time? Where were they holding the front line?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were in the neighbouring villages. But since Kravica is a wooded mountain village, there were ambushes carried out and the village guards were killed at the entrance to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Nikolic, where you were on Christmas day of the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was at home in the village of Opravdici. The day before, I was making plum brandy, because that was our holiday, and so I made this Pecenica so that we could celebrate that holiday the following day. Kravica was attacked from all sides. It was attacked from four sides. All the villages were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go step by step, so please try to answer the questions that I am putting to you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, in your best recollection, when did this attack on your village of Kravica begin on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My wife got up early in the morning at about 5.30 to bake this special bread that we call Cesnica. I stayed in the room to sleep a little bit longer. I didn't know what was going on. I didn't hear anything. And then she entered the room and said, "oh my God, Ratko, get up. We are being attacked from all sides." I said, "What's happening, Marija?" She said, "Well, go out and see what's happening." So I went out, and the village of Sikovici, a small village on the hill, is a place where you have a good view of all the surrounding area. You could see fires everywhere, and there was all kinds of shouting, "Slaughter them," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you do at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. I had two houses. You couldn't go out. Bullets were flying everywhere. My wife -- the entrance to the ground floor, it was between the two houses. She ran into the house. I was immediately wounded in my left leg, right here. And so I ran into the house, she got some cloths, and she managed to bandage me a little bit. And you could already hear things. And I hold her, "Marija, run where you can." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was afraid that I would get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to slow down so that the interpreters can catch all your words. And could I ask you to make a short pause, Mr. Stojanovic, between answer and the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your wife, Marija, manage to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She fled through a wood in the direction of the river Drina, towards Serbia, because there were more refugees who were running from Kravica, so she joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I stayed in my village. I didn't go. I was thinking this is all I have. I don't have anybody left. So what if I get killed. There were five houses in my hamlet. There were no longer any men there. So I stayed in that village for five days longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will stop you there for a moment. Where were you hiding during those five days? Where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was in a little wood, close to my house. There is a large hollow tree there in the woods, and next to that tree there is no path or road or anything. So I crawled inside the tree from the lower side, and that's where I spent the whole day there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you eat? How did you live?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I would go out a little bit when it got dark, and I would observe, look around, so that nobody would catch me. I knew where my potatoes were, so I took a few handfuls of potatoes, and I would put that in the embers of the fire and this is what I used to eat for those five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those five days, did you see enemy soldiers close to your homes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did, yes. First of all, our villages, my own village and the village nearby, were first looted. I saw in the evening when I came that there were tractors and trucks shipping out the food. I had a lot of grain and food which I wasn't using. They took away the livestock, everything that they could take. And then after that, everything was torched. Seven buildings that belonged to me all burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point did they see you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the fifth day, I got out of that tree where I was and I came home to see. I couldn't see or hear anybody. And I wasn't paying attention, and then they shouted, "Halt." And I stopped and it was all over. I was thinking, well, I'm going to die now. When I looked, there was seven of them with seven rifles and they were standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did those seven people look, the ones that captured you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They had white camouflage clothes. They had weapons with them. They didn't saying [as interpreted] anything. They weren't calling each other by their names. They were addressing each other as Mico, Drago. They were not saying Omer, Haso, but Mico, Drago, things like that. Perhaps to avoid being recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After they captured you, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Kravica. My village was 1 kilometre away from Kravica. We reached Kravica, they beat me, they started slapping me, calling me Chetnik. Then we went in the direction of Konjevic Polje. There is a village there that I know. I would commute with Muslims, with Bosniaks, to Zvornik every day when I used to work. Those people knew me. I commuted for 27 years to work, there and back, and we got on well together. So they started to walk towards me, then stopped, and they said, "Ratko, what are you doing here?" I couldn't tell them anything. The van came and it stopped in this crowd of people, women and children and men. A man with a moustache, trimmed moustache, and an automatic rifle got out of the van. Later, I found out that that was Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to stop you there for a little bit. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where this place was where you reached the road and where the van came?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The place is called Lolici. It's a village from the Osmace area in the direction of Konjevic Polje. It's about 3 kilometres away from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after the van stopped and this man came out, whom you learned later was called Zulfo Tursunovic, then what happened to you personally?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He got me to go into the van. There were about 15 of their soldiers there. Naser Oric was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other prisoners in the van except you -- other than you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, there was nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took me up there about 2 kilometres away from Kravica to a village called Jezercica [phoen] because on the left-hand side there was Bratunac. We didn't go to Bratunac. We turned left, then the van stopped, they got out of the van, and then we were going towards Bjeceva, towards Srebrenica, over the hill. We were going on foot. And then when we came down to the Potocari river, there was another van waiting there. They got into the van; me too. They then took me to Srebrenica in this van.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where they brought you first? What building did they bring you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To the old police station building in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We stayed there until the attack on Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber when this attack on Skelani occurred?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think the attack on Skelani took place on the 16th of January. I remember it well because they brought five captured people from Skelani to the Srebrenica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For those of us who don't know too many details about the attack on Skelani, could you please tell us what year that was? The 16th of January of what year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who attacked Skelani?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to what those people who were brought in said - Ilija, he was the only one I knew - it was Naser Oric. I don't know who his commanders were and all of that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And during that time that you were at the police station in Srebrenica, were you interrogated, questioned, was a statement taken from you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The following day I was taken out by a man. I don't know who that was and he asked me what do I have, about my possessions; livestock, food, things like that. Nothing other than that. On the table, there was some salt, a knife, and a pistol in front of him. First he asked me what the knife was for. I just shrugged and said it's used for a man to feed himself and other things. And he said, "No. When you Serbs make crosses" -- I can't remember exactly what he said. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I will ask you something else. Were you asked by anyone during those few days that you spent at the police station if you were a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask me anything. I was wearing civilian clothes. Nobody had summoned me for anything. I didn't have any military clothing. I had a suit, something similar to what I'm wearing now. When I came to the police station the following day, they took my clothes from me, they brought me some boots that were ripped, and they brought me a shirt that didn't even have any sleeves. And they took my new suit from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the people who were guarding you in that facility, where they soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were just wearing civilian clothes, but probably they were policemen because they were guarding us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And from that police station, after the 16th of January 1993, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since there were four of us, it was a small room, 2 X 2, then they brought five more people, then they transferred us between the court and the municipal building to a place where they used to keep coal for the boilers for the municipal building, and that's where they locked us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber how many prisoners were there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were four of us who were there before at the police station, and then these five, so there were nine of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please try to remember, if you can, and could you please tell the Court who you remember, either by name or surname or nickname, who was prisoner together with you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can remember. When I was brought to Srebrenica, I found Popovic Kostadin from Kravica, he was captured before I was and he was brought to Srebrenica. Mico Milovanovic from Sase. Mico and Popovic were killed there in Srebrenica when we were there before my very own eyes. I know when that happened. Then Drago, an elderly man, he was over 80 years old. And there was this one man there. He was taken to hospital. He was wounded in both legs, but I don't remember his name. They took him away. They took him to hospital. Since he could not get up and walk, he walked on his knees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this man by the name of Drago, the elderly man?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago died, because of the beatings, the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, do you remember out of the people who were brought in after the attack of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the village of Skelani, do you remember --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I remember Ilija who was exchanged together with me. Then I know Stanoje, some man who was paralyzed. He couldn't run away. His left leg, right leg. He was exchanged. There is this other guy, I can't remember his name, who was with Kostadin Popovic, who died. I mean, died because of the beating. And two old men were exchanged on the 14th. I mean, February -- no, by the 27th of February. Women, children, then this old Stanoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the conditions like as you stayed there in the room that you described?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Two, three small windows, 50 X 50, bars, no glass, concrete floor. One blanket. We could sit on the floor and cover our heads. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one moment you mentioned women and children. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, when we got up there, we found 14 women and 4 children next door, to the left. I remember this little boy, Branko. He was about 8. I saw him twice now. He's grown up now. They would let him go out a bit. They would let him come to our room a bit. I mean, women and children. You know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with that group of women and children?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were exchanged in January, February. The women, children, and the man, Stanoje. He couldn't walk. He had trouble with his arm and leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in this furnace room, were you questioned at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no way. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody check whether you were a soldier or civilian?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. No one. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see who was in charge and who was in command of these people who were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I did. In the evening when they would come, they would take me out because we had nothing to eat. They really tortured us with this food. We would get three or four mouthfuls of oats and three or four spoonfuls of something that wasn't even cooked, that wasn't salty, that wasn't greasy, nothing. And then in the evening during their shift, this one man would say, "Come on, Nikolic, let's go out and talk." And he said, "They'll beat you less here than there," two or three hours, and then they were lighting fires, and it was very cold in Srebrenica then; 10 or 15 degrees below zero. And we had no clothes. And then he talked to me. He was from Suceska, he was really a good man. I have to say that. He'd bring me this tiny little piece of cornbread, see, like, two fingers, and then he'd take me to toilet and say, "Nikolic, come on. Eat this. I cannot bring this for all of you because I even haven't got enough myself."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you beaten during that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We were beaten every day. Whoever would come in would beat us. There were these two men who beat us regularly. They were with these big glasses. You know, the ones that welders wear, and they had beards, and they were beating us. And I know when I came I was all scarred. See? See this here and here and here on the left side? And when they wanted to exchange the women the next day, the 7th, in the evening, I don't know, at some point in time and during the night, the three of them walked in. The guards let them in, and the guards were the ones who were letting them in to beat us. And they opened the door, and they had this thing made of paper, and then they started beating us one by one. And then I was so hurt here - see, I have all this medical documentation from doctors. All my ribs were broken here. They made us take off the little bit of clothing that we were wearing, and as they beat everyone, we would pass out and then they would pile us up. And then they would bring cold water, and then they'd pour this cold water on us, and that's how it was. When I came to, I don't even know what time it was, I was shivering, and I found this blanket. And I just put it on my head. And then I leaned against the wall. When it dawned, I looked around, and I saw that Kostadin Popovic had died and then this other man from Skelani. The two of them were there, dead. About 10.00 or something like that, I don't know exactly, because Zulfo Tursunovic was commander of the camp up there. I found out later he was the main guy there. He walked around, he had this automatic rifle, like this, over his chest, and then he had this moustache, and then he said, "What happened to you?" Now, what could we say? Could we say, "We were beaten by this one, that one," we don't even know their names, and then they would beat us when he'd leave. And then two other men came afterwards, and then they took out to two dead men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you here and ask you were you able to ask for medical assistance because of the injuries that you had sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We asked but to no avail. I mean, my leg, it was swollen after the beating. Nobody wanted to look at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at one point in time -- or, rather, at any point in time while you were there, did you receive information that you would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that facility?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We were detained in that facility until the exchange, end of February, when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court how many attempts were made for this exchange when you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Two attempts and then I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how these unsuccessful attempts evolved.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ilija was beaten up one evening, the one who was exchanged with me. And then he was taken to hospital. I guess the man couldn't talk, he couldn't speak, nothing. And they didn't really treat him there. They didn't have tablets, medicine, nothing. Ilija was there in hospital. And then this man without an arm walked in. Later on, I found out that this one was nicknamed Mis. And Jakov, from Kalabaca, who Naser brought, they were there for seven months. Naser brought them to Srebrenica to our prison, four men and one woman, Andja, and he said, "Let's see." He looked at us. And then these men were lying there, and, "Let's see who can get up." And then I managed to get up a bit. And he said, "Nikolic, you'll be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you otherwise in that room? Where did you usually stay in that room? Where were you lying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All around. Along the wall. We would lie against the wall. Two or three of us would use one blanket because there weren't many blankets, and we'd just try to cover our heads a bit. Nothing. Concrete floor. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you to get up when the guards would walk in?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They had ordered me, the guards -- I mean, they were civilians, but these guards who were guarding us, they ordered me to sit by the door. Right there. As soon as they let somebody in, that I would have to sit because they said I should say that my name is Ratko and last name is Mladic. Whoever would walk in, I would have to get up and greet them and say I'm Ratko Mladic. But I couldn't. I was so beaten up. I was hungry. My insides were all tied up. And then if I would not get up, then I would be slapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back to one of your answers. You said that at one point in time a woman named Andja was brought in and four men and that they were brought from the village of Kalabaca. What village, this settlement Kalabaca is part of what settlement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sekovici. Kalabaca, Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where had they been until then as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When they told you about this exchange, this attempt to carry out the exchange, was it made?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Twice? No. The first time, I mean, well, it didn't succeed. Up there, Srebrenica, Zeleni Jadar, they call it something. Towards Suceska there was lots of snow. There was this little TAM truck. Its tires were no good. We were supposed to walk for a kilometre, and they took us out and they said we cannot go any further. Ilija and I simply couldn't walk. They dragged us a bit through this snow, and we stood up there, standing about two or three hours in that cold weather, and the man called Mis, without an arm, returned. And he said, "Back to Srebrenica. You're going back to prison." I guess the talks failed or something. I don't know why they took us back. And then after about seven days, he came again. Mico was returned -- no, Ilija was returned to hospital again. And they took me to prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Stojanovic please turn off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He came to prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you please turn off your microphone. Yes. Please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, thank you. Then this second time he came, he said, "Nikolic, let's go for an exchange." And I was glad. We set out again in that same TAM truck, and again it couldn't get through. Again, they pushed us somehow. They dragged us, pushed us, and we walked this 1 kilometre, and then we went on. And then their soldiers, this Muslim Bosniak army, they were on duty. And then further down, there was this - what - Serb army, towards Skelani. And then it was two or three hours that we waited there. Nothing doing. We just stood there in that snow. And then from Skelani, two men appeared, and I guess they raised their hands, whatever, I don't know what the signs were. Then nothing. They talked and then I know full well, this captain who came, who brought their people who were to be exchanged for us, in a truck, and I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will have to stop you just for a moment and ask you to tell us, because this last part of your statement is not recorded. Who is this captain, and who are these persons who brought in their people for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The captain was from our army, the Serb army, from Skelani. And the captain was a driver -- no, no, the other one was a driver. The other one was a driver. The one who brought these people in for a exchange. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, did the exchange take place between the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Then they did exchange us. But they brought oxen and sleds. As far as I can remember, two were alive and one was dead. The dead one was in a coffin. But one did not want to go with this other one. I mean, the cart couldn't go up, and then they were supposed to go down so that these people could go. And then the driver and the captain took the oxen and they went down with the oxen, and they loaded all three of them - I mean, the dead one and the two live ones, they were on the sled and they were brought to the separation line. And then they took the oxen, they gave us to them, and then they took us and they brought us to the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Court to the best of your recollection, what day was that? What date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I know it was towards the end of February because quite a bit of time had gone by already. I don't know what day that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was exchanged with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ilija from Skelani was exchanged with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And tell us, were you able to walk when this was going on in view of everything that you described, everything that you had been through?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult. I weighed 75 kilos before and I dropped down to 40. I had problems with my intestines. We were starving, we were thirsty. Any time we asked to drink some water, they wouldn't bring any to us for three days. Then they would bring us a little plastic pail. There was one guy, bless him, I will never forget him, he would say, "Nikolic, don't drink. That's urine. You will get a temperature." And you could see that the liquid in the pail was yellow, that it wasn't transparent, white.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after the exchange, can you please tell us where you were brought to? Where did the exchange take place, close to the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The place is called Kragljivoda, that is where the boundary was there. There is an intersection that leads to Suceska and Kragljivoda. That's just above Skelani. When we were exchanged, I found out about these two live people and two dead people. We were taken back twice -- actually, what happened was that a cousin of Naser's was killed in Skelani during the attack, so they couldn't find him. So that's why we were taken back twice to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did your family know that there would be an exchange?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't know. They didn't even know that I was in Srebrenica. When I arrived finally after being exchanged -- before that, they didn't know anything. They had lost all contact with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions. I'm almost finished. So I kindly ask for a little bit more patience from you. Can you tell us, were you sent for any medical treatment after that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I went to recover in Zvornik. I went to Vlado Prodanovic. He carried out surgery for my hernia. I had to have a new hip. I couldn't walk. And had to have an artificial limb also. To this day, I have difficulty walking. One of my legs is 5 centimetres shorter now. When they were dragging us to the canal, my leg was injured. The hip joint was damaged in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D05386. Your Honours, by your leave, I would just like to take a moment to consult with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I would ask you to look now in front of you at the screen, at the monitor, and see if you can look. There is a document there. It's a discharge sheet from the Zvornik medical centre. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it states there -- I'm going to try to go quickly through it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is when I was exchanged, when I went for treatment in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there it says, if you can see: Treated between the 1st of March, 1993 and the 14th of March, 1993. And there is a diagnosis there. Is this the medical documentation that you were given once you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And are these papers that you gave to me when we were preparing for you to testify here in this trial?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender document 1D05386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document receives number D1039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another document, please. And that's 1D05385.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, on the left side of the monitor, we can see that it's written in the language that you understand, a document. It's a discharge sheet with your case history.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's issued by the health care centre in Loznica. The date is from 2007. And it's physical therapy following the surgery for a hip replacement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please repeat his question and the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one question regarding these medical documents. Your hip replacement surgery, was that because -- a consequence and needed because of the injuries you sustained while you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document. And it's 65 ter number 1D05385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number D1040.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I see the time. I believe I will be finished with this witness in about 10 or 15 minutes, so perhaps this would be a good moment to take our break, and then I will have a few more questions for the witness regarding events after 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, Mr. Stojanovic, have you inquired with the Prosecution whether there is any challenge to the story of this witness, which is about brutal treatment? I don't hesitate to use that word, that's what he describes, because in general I never found -- well, never. I experienced during the whole of this trial that individual cases of brutal treatment by Muslims to individual Serbs is not really in dispute that these things happened, may even have frequently happened. Have you inquired with the Prosecution whether there was any challenge or any dispute about this story as one perhaps of many stories? Did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In a number of conversations we had, we did discuss the matter of this and similar other witnesses. The Prosecution stated their position about one of them. So for one of those witnesses, there will be no questions. As for this witness, the matter of dispute was whether he was a soldier or a civilian, if we got the information correctly; and also, it's a disputed matter if there were any reasons for the people of Kravica to take revenge. And that's why the Prosecution asked to be able to put specific questions to the witness on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then why didn't you focus on what was in dispute? We have listened, and we didn't want to stop this witness because we see his condition. We didn't want to stop him, but we were flooded with all kind of details, totally unnecessary, to give us a true impression of brutal treatment. You could have done that in not more than 10, at the most 15 minutes, especially where the physical condition of the witness, apparently, is supported by documentation. So why then didn't you focus on what was in dispute? Apparently not that he's in a bad physical condition and that -- I don't know whether that's in dispute, but whether this was caused by ill-treatment, brutal treatment by the Muslim side. Could I ask Ms. Melikian whether there was any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You're correct. In general, there is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also as far as the physical ill-treatment and brutal treatment?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: That is also not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not even raised the issue of relevance. But you could have done in 15 minutes, Mr. Stojanovic. We take the break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. Before we bring the witness back, if I may just say one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you, before you escort the witness into the courtroom, seek my permission. You can get him ready. You need how much time, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you take care that the witness will be standby in one minute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I just made an error on page 25, lines 11 and 12, of the transcript. It states that I said that I had talked to my colleagues from the Prosecution about what was in dispute in the statement of this witness, and I would like to say that I did not discuss with any colleagues from the Prosecution this matter. But this Defence believes that we should be allowed through the viva voce testimony of this witness to have the witness answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you are to focus on matters which are in dispute. You have the right to ask questions to the witness. I never said you are not. Second, you shouldn't tell us that you have discussed the matter with the Prosecution if you had not. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we'll continue. Mr. Stojanovic has a few more questions for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we don't have too many questions now. Just briefly, could you please tell the Trial Chamber if you are suffering from the consequences of the injuries that you sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness told us already, Mr. Stojanovic. And we can see it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you table to tell the Trial Chamber how many people from your village were killed in the attack of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that it was about 48 people who were killed. There were also those who were burnt to death in the houses and their bodies have still not been found to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the population of your village and Kravica and the environs, did they feel the need for retribution because of these casualties caused by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, things were done all the time because Naser Oric and his army destroyed all the villages in the area. There was 17 villages and all of them were burned. Everything was looted. Nothing was left there. Once they looted the things and took them, then they burned all the houses, all the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for this need and expressed desire for revenge? What did they tell you, those people? Was it a result of the things they experienced on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: When you see people with their heads cut off, their legs cut off, after all the things that I heard, there were three or four persons with their heads cut off that were taken to Srebrenica, all kinds of things happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when did you manage to come back to your home?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I managed to return to my house -- well, I have a brother in Mali Zvornik, so I was spending time there. Everything was burned and destroyed back there, so I didn't have anywhere to go back right until Dayton. After Dayton, I received some assistance and I built something, 64 square metres. So I think that that was it. My grandmother is living there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, thank you very much for all your answers, for your willingness to come and testify. This Defence has no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Melikian, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Melikian, you'll find her to your right. Ms. Melikian is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in your testimony you'd just said at line -- transcript page 28, that it was approximately 48 people who were killed in your village on the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the attack on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And does that number include soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were no soldiers. They were all civilians. Mostly these were civilians that were escaping. All of them were civilians, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Could we please turn to 65 ter 4415.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And just as it comes up, as we look at the first page of this document, we see that it's -- well, just as a bit of background this was a report that was seized from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters by the Office of the Prosecutor in February 1998. And we see on the first page that it says: "The Situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina Before the War." This is a detailed and chronological report of the events leading up to the war and the formation of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And if we can please turn to page 11 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Just to see this section header in the middle of the page that says: "Description, Characteristics, and Results of Combat and Other Combat Tasks the Brigade has Executed During its Existence." We'll just be taking a look at some of the text in this section.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: So if we could please turn to page 15 in the English and 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And if we just look about two-thirds of the way down in the English and at the top of the page in the B/C/S, we see that it says: "The Muslims knew about the situation among the Serbs, which is why they hurried with the new attacks to take Kravica as soon as possible. They planned to execute their main and decisive attack on Christmas, 7 January 1993." And further down, we see: "In the early morning of 7 January 1993 on Christmas at dawn, the attack on Kravica was launched from almost all directions."

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: If we could please then turn to page 17 in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet. Could you tell us from where you were reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: One second. I'm sorry, there it is. In the bottom third, it starts, in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now found the 7th of January, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And if we could then please turn to page 17 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And looking at the top of the page in the English and about the middle of the page in the B/C/S, we see that it's written: "The grim outcome for the people of Kravica on Christmas 1993 was 35 killed and 36 wounded soldiers and 11 civilians." It's the Prosecution's position that this report accurately represents the number of casualties that day and that, in fact, 35 soldiers were killed and 11 civilians were killed. Do you agree that the figures reported here are accurate, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know that there is this monument in Kravica now, and I read about this, you know, those 48 that I know about, and it also says so on and the monument. These 48 are civilians. I cannot tell you anything about soldiers. I was not there. I cannot say anything. As for these 48, I know exactly. There is this monument there now, and it says "civilian victims, 48 of them." It's written there. As for the soldiers, I really don't know. I really cannot tell you anything about that because I wasn't there. I was already up there then, because this was after two months. For two months you couldn't go into Kravica because Naser held Kravica. Birds were eating away. Things happened to people. People's heads were cut off. And this relative of mine had his head cut off, and if it wasn't for his dog who was there watching him, the birds would have eaten him up. I didn't dare go there and -- I mean, I didn't know how many. I mean, I see it on the monument now, the civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one question, Witness. Is the monument the only source of your information that the people who died were 48 and that they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't need to explain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I just have two additional questions for you. Do you recall testifying previously at the Tribunal in December 2004 in the case of the Prosecutor versus Mr. Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: And were you called by the Prosecution in that case?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes. I mean, they came from The Hague and then they prepared me there. I think it was them. As far as I can remember, there was nobody else. There was nobody else who contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Melikian. Any further questions in re-examination? Mr. Nikolic, the Chamber has no further questions for you either, which means that this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and that were put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may Ms. Hasan and I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Ms. Melikian. You didn't tender the last document. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are trying to find out whether the next witness, which, if I understand well, is Mr. Vujic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has yet arrived or not because he was expected at 11.30 but he may have arrived early.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we asked the service to bring him earlier since we learned that there wouldn't be many questions from the Prosecution for the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, you'll cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you now to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujic. Please be seated. Mr. Vujic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. In a minute he will stand. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask the usher to provide Mr. Vujic with his statement in paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a clean copy, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to inspect, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please just slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Drasko Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, at one point in time did you give a statement to the members of the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D0502516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. 0502516?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake. 1D02516. I apologise. And we need the last page. Since this is a statement from the Karadzic case, there is no first page signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujic, on the last page of your statement that is on the screen before you right now, can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in your statement, is it recorded properly in relation to what you had said?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, what is recorded in this statement, is that truthful?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything I said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer me in the same way? Would your answers be the same like those provided in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would basically give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender Mr. Vujic's statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement receives number D1041.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would read the statement summary of Mr. Vujic, and I would have questions for him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Drasko Vujic was mobilised in late 1991 and sent as a member of the 5th Battalion of the 343 JNA Brigade to Slavonia, where he stayed for 45 days. After that, he went back to Prijedor. And when the crisis in Prijedor broke out, he started forming a unit from the Urije area, or Prijedor 2 area, local community. This unit numbered about 900 to 1200 men, many of whom were non-Serbs who joined the unit voluntarily. In the morning of 30th of May, 1992, Muslim armed units attacked Mr. Vujic's soldiers from a park located between the two underpasses and from a nearby firm. One of his soldiers was killed in the attack, while the others reacted to the surprise and put up resistance. During the clash, the Muslims fired at an ambulance car that was on its way to town and seriously wounded the driver. After one hour of fighting, the Muslim units were pushed back and withdrew towards the river Sana. During the fighting, one enemy soldier was captured. He wore a camouflage uniform with a green headband, a Cherokee hair-style, and Islamic markings. After revealing that Prijedor was attacked by several armed groups from different directions, the prisoner was escorted to the garrison and handed over to the security organs. After this episode, the battalion did not take part in combat operations until September 1992, when most of the battalion was sent to the Gradacac front line while a small part received the task of mopping out Mount Kurevo, where Muslim units were based. One of the soldiers who took part in the fighting at Kurevo was wounded, while one other died. During the summer of 1992, the battalion's patrols were present in the vicinity of the mosque in Puharska, when the mosque was destroyed in an explosion. Mr. Vujic personally helped the people who had been injured, among whom there was a Muslim man who was put in Mr. Vujic's car and taken to the hospital, where he received medical treatment. The soldiers who were on patrol were severely shocked and some suffered hearing damage. Mr. Vujic did everything he could to reassure the residents of Puharska and to prevent any further attempts at disturbing them. In 1992, various Serbian paramilitary units roamed around Prijedor municipality, causing great problems to both the Muslim and the Serbian population. Mr. Vujic personally arrested a member of this Suva Rebra unit, one of the paramilitary formations active in the Prijedor area. The paramilitary soldier was disarmed, tied up, and later escorted to the prison in Gradiska. In 1995, Mr. Vujic became a member of the SDS and then he became vice-president of the Municipal Board and an assemblyman in the municipal assembly. That was statement summary, Your Honours, and I would probably ask -- is it break time or we have still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not break time yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will continue with my questions with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. We have another 20 minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would start with one document which we proposed as non-associated exhibit, and it is in our system under the number 1D04952.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have before us a document, Mr. Vujic, that has no translation. So this is what I'm going to ask you. Could you please read out the name of the document?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: "List of Persons of Non-Serb Ethnicity Who Were Members of the 3rd Motorised Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you also please read out for us the next line that denotes the columns. So what is written there, the next line?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The first column is "number," the second is "surname, father's name, and name" of each and every member of the unit, the third is "year of birth," and the fourth is the period that was spent in the unit from the beginning until the end of the participation of each and every individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, who wrote up this document?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I drew up this document from the database that I still have about the participation of soldiers who were members of the 3rd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is easy for us to understand this column that says number, and also the one that says last name, father's name, and name, and the year of birth. The last column, though, that says "period of engagement," how did you make these entries, Mr. Vujic? How did you enter data there?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: In our military records, each and every member, once he reported to the unit, has the date of his arrival recorded, and the second part of the column refers to the date when he left the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask one question at this point in time, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vujic, if you look at item 21, there is a name and he is listed as having been admitted into the army on the 6th of July, 1993 and he leaves from his duties on the same day. What might be the background of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, obviously what happened was that the soldier was sent by the ministry to the 3rd Battalion. Upon arriving in the unit, he brought a document that freed him from participation in the unit. On the basis of the document that he had then, he was released on the same day and returned home. The decision of the ministry was abided by, but in the meantime he obtained a document that freed him from service. And I, as commander, freed him on that basis and let him go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujic, what are the reasons for the members of your unit not to be engaged anymore?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: There are several reasons. This document shows that there were certain individuals who were engaged in the unit from the first until the very last day. You can see that some arrived on the very first day. And then after a year or two, or at some point in time before the end they left the unit, and that was possible only if such a person would receive an assignment to go to a different unit because of the VS that he had, the military occupational speciality, or if somebody was ill or wounded. Unfortunately, some people were also killed. And there were some other reasons why people left this unit before the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether the dates you are giving, is that purely on the basis of administrative documents, or did you also verify whether they were actually on duty during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the basis of the official documents of the battalion, that's how I did this. The battalion has a book, VOB-8, and everything is clearly recorded there, and each and every one of these dates has to match the dates that are in the VOB-8 that was handed over to the ministry. There must be no difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that there shouldn't be any difference, but did you verify whether there was any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I have a copy of the VOB about the participation of all the participants, not from VOB-8 but from my own records before I submitted the VOB, I copied the data into the VOB. So when we are talking about the status and the length of service of each of these soldiers, not only them but all those who were in the battalion - and I must say that 2.540 of them passed through the battalion during the war - none of them had any remarks regarding the length of service and participation in the unit, because it does correspond to the official records in the VOB-8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's still all on the basis of administrative documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the basic and only valid document, the VOB-8. Everything else are records which I, as the commander, as well as subordinate officers of the companies and the platoons, kept. But they all tally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujic, did you know any of these people or all of these people personally, and do you have any personal knowledge that they were members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew most of these people personally. I didn't know a small number of them by their first name and last name. I have this very good characteristic, that I can recall faces very easily. So on the basis of that, I definitely do remember them, although I might have forgotten some of their names. However, these are only those who spent a very short time in the unit. For example, the Workers Battalion, which was added to my unit for brief periods of time, perhaps a period of 30 or 45 days or a maximum period of 60 days, that category of fighter perhaps means that I didn't know some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see that the column ends with the year 1996. And you see there are no records from 1997 or 1998. Could you please explain why the last entries are from 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The column shows dates up to 1996, which means that until 1996 the unit functioned officially. In 1996, most of the fighters were demobilised. I can say as the commander that just a few of my associates remained in order that we could finish up with the MTS and to complete all the documents that we were obliged to present to the garrison or the brigade command. All the other personnel was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did these members of your battalion come from? From which area?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: These members mostly came from the replenishment area of this wartime battalion, which included the local communes of Urije, Puharska, Orlovaca, Orlovci, Garevci, and Cirkin Polje. There were a few of those who came from other parts of the municipality and who joined this unit. Most of them were from the replenishment area of the local communes that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is all found in the statement. Please proceed. Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, and where were the families of these men who were members of your unit and who were not ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that they were from this zone of replenishment, their families were living in their own homes. They didn't go anywhere. They were together with us. They saw the unit off together with us, they greeted it when it came back, and they went through the good times and the bad times together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the fighters from your unit of Serb ethnicity towards those who were not of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: In this unit, there were no differences at all between Serb fighters and of those of other ethnic groups. We went to the front together, we returned together, we shared the same fate. At the front, we slept in the same trenches, shared the same food, drank the same drink. We helped each other. And please believe me when I say that in times of crisis, these are events that can tell stories from wartime when co-fighters help each other in difficult situations. There was no difference between members of different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would offer this document to be MFI'd since there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we first see the last page of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the third page. Can we see the third page, please. Actually, the fourth page. The last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So the list ended with number 133; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D1042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1042 is admitted -- no, is marked for identification, apologies, pending a translation. But there are no objections, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think now it's a break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's still even five minutes before break time. But if you find this is a suitable moment, then we will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would change the topics, so yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a good reason. Mr. Vujic, we will take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher. We would like to see you back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, please focus on the Court rather than on the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is with us, I just want to inform the Chamber that now we released the translation for D1042 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the -- could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The list. Yes. Then there are no objections, Mr. Zec, you told us. Therefore, Madam Registrar, the English translation may be added to D1042 and D1042 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you know what doc ID the English translation has. If not, the Defence will inform you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujic, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 6 of your statement. And that's on page 2. In that paragraph of your statement, you say that before the fighting and searches, you proposed and offered to the Muslim TO to hand over their weapons to avoid unwanted clashes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Where did you go and did you go anywhere in order to negotiate about all these matters?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I insisted a number of times on meetings between the leadership of the Muslim side and us so that we could meet and discuss like men, review the situation, and see what the best thing would be for us to do. I did not hesitate to go to their territory, conditionally speaking, for this purpose. One of our meetings was held in their TO headquarters even. That's where we met and held our talks on the subject of how to adapt to the conditions and avoid any civilian casualties or further clashes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you -- with the same purpose of avoiding clashes, did you approach Serbs also to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the Serbs formed a military unit which had access, meaning that those that I talked to could also come and be a member of that unit. So those were the reasons why I went to talk with those who didn't want to join the official unit. I was asking them to hand over their weapons so that we wouldn't have to wage war with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this paragraph doesn't say you approached those who didn't want to hand over weapons. It says you approached the Muslim TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I contacted their superiors, their officers who were responsible for them, for what they were doing there, because they were the ones who were carrying out the orders of those that I was holding the talks with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the TO was also a unit that is there to protect the community, and you're saying the Serbs were part of the army and that's why you didn't go to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're talking about an interethnic conflict in this case, the Territorial Defence would not have any purpose at all, unless we are talking about an opposing side. Then each side would be important. If it was a war where everyone together would be carrying out the orders of the superior command, of the corps command, the army units and so on, there would be no need for the Territorial Defence to exist at all.
